hints: Focus on what makes a carbon chiral, four different groups attached to the same carbon, then draw out the carbon skeleton first.
Sketch 2,2,4,5-tetramethylhexan-3-ol carefully, C3 has the OH, C2 has two methyls, C4 has one methyl and C5 has one methyl.
Check C3, C4 and C5 one by one for four different groups, and watch out for any carbon that carries two identical methyl groups.
walkthrough:
**Draw the parent chain**

Great start, let us build the molecule. Hexan-3-ol means a 6-carbon chain with OH on C3.

$$ \text{C1 - C2 - C3(OH) - C4 - C5 - C6} $$

**Add the four methyl branches**

Now add 2,2,4,5-tetramethyl. That means two $\text{CH}_3$ on C2, one $\text{CH}_3$ on C4 and one $\text{CH}_3$ on C5. Fill remaining bonds with H.

**Recall the chiral test**

A chiral carbon has four different groups attached. No plane of symmetry, no two identical groups. Carbons with two H or two $\text{CH}_3$ can never be chiral.

**Test C3 and C4**

C3 is bonded to $\text{H}$, $\text{OH}$, $\text{C(CH}_3)_3$ on the left (C2 side), and a $\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$ type group on the right (C4 side). All four are different, so C3 is chiral. C4 is bonded to $\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_3$, C3 side $\text{CH(OH)C(CH}_3)_3$ and C5 side $\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$. All four are different, so C4 is also chiral.

**Rule out the others**

C2 has two identical $\text{CH}_3$ branches, so not chiral. C5 is bonded to $\text{H}$, C4, $\text{CH}_3$ (branch) and C6 which is also $\text{CH}_3$. Two identical methyls, so not chiral. C1 and C6 are $\text{CH}_3$ groups. That leaves exactly 2 chiral centres.

options.A: 1 is too few. Many students spot only C3 (the carbon with OH) as chiral and miss C4. C4 also has four different groups: H, methyl, the C3 fragment and the C5 fragment.
options.B: 2 is correct. C3 and C4 are both chiral. C3 carries H, OH, tert-butyl-like C2 group and C4 group. C4 carries H, methyl, C3 group and C5 group. C2 and C5 each carry two identical methyl groups so are achiral.
options.C: 3 is incorrect. This comes from counting C5 as chiral as well as C3 and C4. C5 looks substituted but it is bonded to two identical CH3 groups (C6 and its methyl branch), so it fails the four-different-groups test.
options.D: 4 is incorrect. This comes from assuming every branched carbon (C2, C3, C4, C5) is chiral. C2 has two identical methyl branches and C5 has two identical methyl groups, so neither can be a chiral centre.
